enrichment.short_title: Relocation contract formed on capped acceptance of earlier per-load quotation, not later fixed-price proposal
key_facts: Pickfords faxed Celestica a budget quotation on 13 September 2001 based on £890 per vehicle load plus extras, estimated at about £100,000 total.
On 27 September Pickfords sent a detailed fixed-price proposal for £98,760 incorporating standard terms and conditions.
Celestica's fax of 15 October 2001 confirmed an order by reference to the 13 September fax and added 'Not to exceed 100K'; Pickfords performed the relocation work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court recorder's decision on which offer was accepted and contract terms.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; contract held to be on the first-offer terms subject to the £100,000 cap, not the fixed-price proposal.
enrichment.ratio: A later inconsistent offer may impliedly revoke an earlier offer where the documents show a superseding regime rather than alternative quotations; an acceptance referring expressly to the first offer and capping liability at the earlier budget figure creates a counter-offer accepted by conduct, even where the parties argued different analyses.
legal_issues: Whether the 27 September proposal revoked the 13 September offer
Which offer was accepted by Celestica's 15 October fax
Effect of the 'Not to exceed 100K' wording on contract price
Whether 'CONFIRMATION' pointed to the second offer

enrichment.short_title: Saudi embassy employee refused permission to appeal state immunity bar to unfair dismissal claim
key_facts: Mr Hassan, an Egyptian interpreter in the Saudi Military Attaché's department in London, claimed constructive unfair dismissal after refusing less favourable 1998 contracts imposing tax and NI obligations.
The employment tribunal held the claim failed because s.16(1)(a) State Immunity Act 1978 disapplied the employment exception in s.4 for members of a diplomatic mission.
The EAT dismissed an estoppel argument, finding estoppel cannot enlarge tribunal jurisdiction over a statutory immunity bar.

enrichment.ratio: Where s.16(1)(a) State Immunity Act 1978 applies, the employment tribunal lacks jurisdiction and estoppel cannot be used to circumvent the statutory bar; 'members of a mission' takes its meaning from Article 1 Vienna Convention and includes administrative and technical staff.

enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal wrongly treated joint spousal commission arrangement as illegal tax evasion
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Colen, shareholder-employees of Cebrian (UK) Ltd, claimed unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and unpaid commission after dismissal in June 1995.
They had long received low basic salaries plus 10% sales commission shared between spouses in a tax-efficient manner advised by accountants.
The employment tribunal found Mrs Colen had no contractual commission entitlement and that the contracts were tainted by revenue fraud, dismissing all claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Employment Appeal Tribunal decision reversing the tribunal on illegality but remitting quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; employment tribunal decision held flawed; matter remitted to assess commission and notice remedies on basis of joint entitlement.
enrichment.ratio: Illegality in performance of an otherwise lawful joint commission contract does not automatically render the whole employment contract unenforceable; the employer bore the burden of proving fraud on the Revenue and the tribunal erred in finding Mrs Colen had no contractual share in commission, especially given conceded joint entitlement before 1988 and insufficient evidence of any 1988 change.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Colen was contractually entitled to a share of commission
Whether tax-efficient splitting of joint commission rendered contracts illegal
Burden of proof where illegality is pleaded in employment claims
How remedies should be assessed for jointly earned commission

key_facts: Paul Kelleher damaged a temporary statue of Lady Thatcher in the Guildhall Gallery with a cricket bat and metal stanchion to publicise anti-globalisation and political concerns.

Kelleher admitted the damage and sought to rely on political motives and concern for his son's future under section 5 lawful excuse.

enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe despite improper direction to convict.
enrichment.ratio: Lawful excuse under section 5 Criminal Damage Act 1971 requires destruction or damage objectively done in order to protect property or a proprietary right or interest in immediate need of protection by reasonable means; political belief and generalised fears for the future do not engage the defence, but even where a judge wrongly directs conviction a safe verdict may stand where the evidence overwhelmingly establishes guilt and no defence could succeed.

enrichment.short_title: Juvenile murderer's 16-year minimum term upheld despite welfare challenge and oral hearing request

statutes_considered.title: United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child

key_facts: Anthony Dudson was convicted aged 16 of murder in the torture and killing of Suzanne Capper and sentenced to detention at Her Majesty's pleasure with an original 18-year tariff.
Following T and V v UK and transitional procedures, the Lord Chief Justice reset the minimum term to 16 years in January 2002, recognising progress in custody.
Dudson challenged the reset tariff for failure to reflect welfare under s.44 Children and Young Persons Act 1933 and for lack of an oral hearing before the Lord Chief Justice.

enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; 16-year minimum term not unlawful; no entitlement to oral hearing on the facts and any such right was waived; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: When resetting a s.53(1) tariff after Venables and T v UK, the Lord Chief Justice undertook a fresh judicial tariff-setting exercise in which welfare is one factor but does not require building in speculative exceptional progress or the lowest possible term; Article 6 does not require an oral hearing where detailed written representations fully address the issues, and continued pursuit of written submissions may waive an earlier conditional request for a hearing.

Whether absence of periodic review required a lower minimum term
